Long-horizon exploration with heightened reward sensitivity and dopamine/frontostriatal remodeling. This shows up behaviorally as an adolescent-specific peak in contingency-based switching (reversal learning) via less perseveration and more stochastic choice behavior, and that this mode of "undirected" exploration increases environmental sampling and behavioral variability. Their developmental "goal" claim is that this sampling is useful because adolescence coincides with encountering a broader diversity of contexts (transition-to-independence), and the resulting "brain state exploration" gives the system chances to test/identify brain states that support reliable, efficient cognition later.

Looking closely at frontal activity, Jonkman (2006) found a linear increase in no-go P3 amplitude (a positive wave 300 - 500 ms after stimulus presentation) across development: Children ages 6-7 showed no P3 activity, children ages 9-10 showed limited P3 activity in frontal-central electrodes, and young adults showed broad P3 activity across frontal and frontal-central electrodes (see also Jonkman el al., 2003). P3 activity has been interpreted to index the allocation of attentional resources during stimulus engagement, with greater activity representing greater resource allocation (Polich, 1987). In contrast, the no-go N2 response (a negative wave 150 - 400 ms after stimulus presentation) decreased across the same age span, with the largest decrease in amplitude occurring between ages 6 and 10.

Kwon, Reiss, and Menon (2002) reported a quantitative linear increase in activity within a fronto-parietal network, including ventral and dorsal regions of the PFC, from ages 7 to 22 while performing a visuo-spatial WM task (n-back task). The authors note that the increased activity within right-lateralized dorsal PFC likely subserves the maturation of visuo-spatial attention and executive processes, whereas the increased activity within a left-lateralized fronto-parietal network subserves the maturation of a phonological rehearsal system. Scherf, Sweeney, and Luna (2006) reported both qualitative changes (location of activation) and quantitative changes (amount of activation) in the neural response underlying visuospatial working memory from childhood (Mage = 11.2) through adulthood (Mage = 29.5). During childhood, activation occurred in qualitatively different premotor regions and also in the lateral cerebellum, which was absent in later development. Also during childhood, there was quantitatively greater activity in ventromedial regions, including the thalamus and basal ganglia. Adolescence (Mage = 15.7) brought a shift in activity to frontal regions, including the right dorsolateral PFC. Finally, from adolescence to adulthood activity became more localized and lateralized as left dorsolateral PFC activation increased and right dorsolateral PFC activation decreased. Moreover, activity increased substantially in the as anterior cingulated (described as qualitative change by the authors). The end result of these changes (quantitative and qualitative, progressive and regressive) from childhood to adulthood is a functionally-specialized visuospatial WM neural network (see Klingberg, Forssberg, and Westerberg, 2002, for similar changes from age 9 to18 on a visuo-spatial WM task). Recent longitudinal imaging relates connectivity to cognition (Figure) 20. A 2026 longitudinal ABCD analysis found brain-network connectivity increasingly predictive of cognition across early adolescence (Figure).

Increased WM also correlates with structural neural indices, such as the maturation of white matter (i.e., the myelination of neuronal axons), measured by DTI. Nagy, Westerberg, and Klingberg (2004) reported that the development of visuo-spatial WM from age 8 to 18 correlated with myelination in regions primarily of the frontal lobe close to the parietal lobe (superior and inferior left frontal lobe), whereas the development of reading ability correlated with myelination in the left temporal lobe. Thus, during late childhood and adolescence, the maturation of specific cognitive functions is linked to the maturation of specific neural circuits, rather than to global brain maturation.

Rubia and her colleagues (Rubia et al., 2006) reported increased activation in inferior frontal, parietal, and anterior cingulate regions, but decreased DL-PFC activation across adolescence during shifting. They proposed that the increased activity in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) reflects the maturation of conflict monitoring processes, whereas the increased DL-PFC activation in younger participants reflects compensatory neural activity

Key Principles for This Window

Protracted Prefrontal Development: The extended timeline of PFC maturation (to  25) creates both vulnerability (risky decisions) and opportunity (extended plasticity).

Experience-Expectant vs. Experience-Dependent: This period relies heavily on experience-dependent plasticity; the brain is sculpted by the specific learning experiences encountered.

Use-Dependent Specialization: Pruning eliminates unused connections; the activities pursued during this window shape the adult cognitive architecture.

Social Context Sensitivity: The adolescent brain is particularly tuned to social information, making peer influence and social learning especially potent.

Identity-Cognition Integration: Cognitive development becomes increasingly tied to identity formation; what one chooses to learn and become shapes who one is.

The extended trajectory for long-horizon planning maps onto the protracted maturation of frontoparietal circuitry. Frontopolar cortex (BA 10)–the apex of the rostrocaudal abstraction gradient–supports cognitive branching: maintaining a superordinate goal while executing and monitoring subgoals. Dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC) supports proactive goal maintenance and rule representation. Anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) handles effort allocation, conflict monitoring, and detecting when outcomes diverge from predictions–the "alarm system" for plan failures. Hippocampus and the broader default mode network support episodic future simulation, enabling the constructive assembly of prospective scenarios from remembered elements. Basal ganglia circuits support hierarchical action selection, gating, and the initiation of cached routines. Because the most temporally extended, abstract levels of the goal hierarchy depend on the slowest-maturing anterior regions, long-horizon planning is among the last capacities to fully mature.
